newsitem.title: GERMANY: East Germans paddle to flooded homes by canoe.
newsitem.headline: East Germans paddle to flooded homes by canoe.

text.p: None of the residents of this village beside the River Oder on Germany's eastern border ever dreamed of having to paddle a canoe through a swamp to see home again.
But, for dozens of families in Germany's flood zone along the waterway, this is the only way to assess damage to their flooded homes, businesses and farms for claims on insurance or relief aid.
While minor flooding is practically an annual event, nobody here was prepared for this year's summer deluge, which they have dubbed the "flood of the century".
Many, including sheep-farmer Joerg Krause, 31, were not fully insured for the worst possibilities.

Krause bought 270 hectares (670 Acres) of grazing land four years ago and has 1,400 sheep and lambs. When the dike holding back the swollen River Oder broke one morning three weeks ago, all his land disappeared under the raging waters.

"I evacuated the sheep before the dike broke. But it all happened so quickly I only had time to get the most important things to safety," he said on Thursday during a visit to his water-logged home in a German army rubber dingy.
"I managed to rescue my tractor but most of the other tools and equipment are ruined," Krause said, adding that this damage would amount to as much as 40,000 marks ($21,100).

That did not include his house, the sheep shed -- a new one would cost 150,000 marks -- the barn and 150 tonnes of hay. "I just haven't had time to calculate losses to my business and damage. But they will be substantial".

Krause's farm is one of 30 farms in the area whose survival is threatened by the floods, according to the federal farm ministry in Bonn. Floods have ruined 12,000 hectares (29,000 acres) of farmland, including crops and pastures.

Chancellor Helmut Kohl pledged 500 million marks in flood relief aid saying aid would be forthcoming and "unbureacratic". The federal and regional governments have set aside 40 million marks for immediate aid for stricken residents.

The European Commission, the European Union's executive body, has given three million marks to help clear the devastated area and pledged another 86 million marks from EU funds earmarked as regional aid. Germany set aside 200 million marks for low-interest credits.

But, Krause said, while he managed to claim 800 marks of a maximum entitlement of 2,000 marks per family for immediate aid for flood victims, applying for a 10,000-mark one-off business relief entitlement was fraught by red tape.
"Let's wait and see how long it takes," he said.

Germany has escaped the worst of floods that killed more than 100 people in the neighbouring Czech Republic and Poland last month and devastated vast swathes of land, towns, farms and villages, causing billions of dollars-worth of damage.
The greatest disaster Germans feared was that the Oderbruch basin which lies below the river would be flooded and nearly all its 19,000 residents would be made homeless.

Now that the river is retreating and the danger of renewed flooding seems a dim prospect, officials met on Thursday to discuss flood damage, the worst of which was here in the Ziltendorf basin, south of Frankfurt an der Oder.

Six villages were partially or totally submerged, 7,200 hectares (18,000 acres) inundated and 300 residents evacuated. Officials say it is impossible to asses damage and pollution before the water has gone but fear it will be billions of marks.

Flood waters receded for the fourth day leaving a trail of mud, dead fish and unidentified objects. The smell of rotting vegetation hangs in the air. What was once fertile farmland has been turned into mosquito-ridden swampland.
"I need a permit before I can plant grass here again for grazing the sheep. But if officials say the land is too polluted, then I may not be allowed to do this," Krause said.
